results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The intro reader predicted all ten sections in the spec's order, the three kinds of evidence (dated provider documentation, the Larkfield case and Mila's payment, first-principles reasoning) and the plain instructional tone; its only doubts (why a sender section, how the two comparisons differ) are minor.
46 of 46 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the aligned spec paragraph, in the spec's order; the three callouts align to nothing.

5 units were marked two_ideas (Introduction ¶2, At-Least-Once ¶1, Contracts ¶1, Signatures ¶3, When It Goes Wrong ¶2); in each the two halves are parts of the one controlling idea the spec declares (placing the chapter; event and webhook and why they exist; the acknowledgement term; how Adyen authenticates; recovery failing), so none holds two controlling ideas.
Every body unit ties to one of C1-C6; introduction and conclusion units frame or synthesize them.

results.finding: The promises table follows the paragraph with no sentence introducing it or saying what it shows, and two rows (a signed event came from the provider; not every change has an event) rest on nothing the section has said; both flow readers stopped at them (A item 8, B item 5). All other tables, the four figures and the quotations are introduced or followed by a sentence or caption saying what they show.

results.quote: The same contract applies on Adyen, with the confirming record changed.
results.finding: That Larkfield also takes payments through Adyen, and that Mila's payment is one of them, is never stated before this point (the introduction's Mila paragraph names no provider, although the spec's evidence for it does); only flow reader B reported it.
The introduction opens on the dated incident, reverses the direction of the previous chapters, states the claim and gives the roadmap; none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion sorts what is established, what depends on context and the author's position, then questions and the hand-off; it does not open with 'in conclusion', add a subtopic, or end on a rephrased thesis alone.

The synthesis bullet maps each receiver step to the limit it answers (deadline, repetition, disorder and staleness, window), which no single section states, and the 'silence is a state of its own' and 'two windows' bullets say why it matters.

results.quote: Silence is a state of its own. A system that can say “unknown, checking” fails more gently than one that must choose between paid and unpaid.
results.finding: The conclusion never returns to the members turned away on 14 September 2026: neither the incident, Larkfield nor the nine hours of silence is named in "What to Take Away", "Questions to Ask" or the hand-off, and the declared callback (retries delivered every event; treating silence as unknown would have kept the doors open) is absent. This bullet is where it would sit.

The cold reader gives both recoveries as expected: Stripe's early events are past their retries, so list them from the Events API, run them through the same handler and read every pending payment; Adyen's queue arrives as a burst, so store and acknowledge first and check against the settlement reports; duplicates removed and arrival order ignored at both.

The cold reader concludes nothing from arrival order, reads the object at Stripe, orders by event date and applies only allowed state-machine transitions at Adyen, and lets a repeat meet the unique key.

The sender section states "Neither Stripe nor Adyen has published how its webhook sender is built", labels what follows "reference-architecture inference ... not an account of either company's system", and closes with an INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED block.

The draft uses the ledger's figures (Monday 14 September 2026, 9 hours, 3,200 memberships, 460 tickets), says the retries repaired the data, and says K2 addresses the reading of silence (re-read, sweep, 'being checked').
